Battle of Britain. The Battle of Britain was an aerial campaign from July to October 1940 in which the German Luftwaffe sought to achieve air superiority over the British Isles as a precondition for invading England in an operation codenamed Sea Lion. The Royal Air Force, defending with the Supermarine Spitfire and Hawker Hurricane fighters, repulsed the Luftwaffe's sustained bombing offensive and fighter sweeps. Germany's failure to defeat the RAF ended Hitler's plans for invasion and preserved Britain as an independent power, symbolizing resistance to Nazi domination.

After defeating France in June 1940, Hitler ordered the Luftwaffe to destroy the RAF and secure air superiority for a cross-Channel invasion. RAF Fighter Command was led by Air Chief Marshal Hugh Dowding, while Germany's Luftwaffe was commanded by Hermann Göring. Britain had radar, called Chain Home, a crucial advantage in detecting incoming German aircraft. German pilots faced twenty-two-minute fights over hostile territory, whereas British pilots faced only five minutes. This meant that downed British pilots could bail out and fight again, while German pilots were lost to the enemy.

The Luftwaffe began with attacks on shipping and coastal targets, then by August switched to bombing RAF airfields, radar stations, and aircraft factories. Daily dogfights raged over the Channel and southern England as the RAF flew over one thousand sorties daily, replacing losses at a rate the Luftwaffe could not match. The Germans suffered unsustainable pilot and aircraft losses. By October, Göring admitted the campaign had failed and switched to night bombing, the start of the Blitz.

The RAF's victory forestalled German invasion and kept Britain in the war as an independent base for future American entry and operations against Hitler's Europe. The battle is remembered for fighter pilot heroism, the role of radar and intelligence, and Churchill's famous words: never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few.
